title: Control & Protection
summary: Keeping load inside what the system can survive. 6 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Rate Limiting — Capping how many requests a caller may make in a window, to protect capacity and enforce fairness.
Backpressure — Letting a saturated consumer slow its producer, so queues stay bounded instead of absorbing an overload until something breaks.
Circuit Breaker — Tripping a dependency call to fail fast after repeated failures, then probing periodically to see whether it has recovered.
Retry with Backoff & Jitter — Re-attempting a failed call on an exponentially increasing, randomised delay, so transient failures heal without synchronising the fleet.
Load Shedding — Deliberately dropping or degrading lower-priority work under overload so the system serves its most important traffic instead of failing at everything.
Bulkhead Isolation — Partitioning resources — thread pools, connections, even fleets — so one dependency or tenant cannot consume everything.

questions.prompt: Rate Limiting vs Backpressure vs Load Shedding — what decides between them?
points: Backpressure — Rate limiting protects you from callers; backpressure tells callers to slow down because you are full.
Load Shedding — When you must drop work by priority under overload rather than by per-caller quota.
Rate Limiting — Capping how many requests a caller may make in a window, to protect capacity and enforce fairness.
questions.answer: Backpressure: Rate limiting protects you from callers; backpressure tells callers to slow down because you are full. Load Shedding: When you must drop work by priority under overload rather than by per-caller quota.

questions.prompt: Rate Limiting appears in 7 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Web Crawler — Per-domain politeness. The crawler caps its own request rate per host — a limiter pointed at itself rather than at incoming callers.
Design a Distributed Rate Limiter — The problem itself. Every decision here is about where the counter lives and how exact it needs to be across a fleet of gateways.
Design a Webhook Delivery System — Delivery attempts per receiver endpoint are capped, so retries toward a struggling customer do not turn into an attack on them.
Design a Content Moderation Pipeline — Caps per-uploader submission rate — the cheapest defence against bulk spam, applied before any model spends compute on the content.
Design an Authentication & Session Service — Login attempts per account and per IP, the primary defence against credential stuffing and brute force.

Design a Sanctions Screening System — Escalations are throttled into the review queue rather than at the matcher, because matching is cheap and the humans are the bottleneck that a list delta would otherwise flood.
Design a Human Review Queue — Admission into the queue is metered per lane, so a 500K-item batch dump drains gradually instead of displacing the live stream that has deadlines attached.

questions.prompt: Backpressure vs Load Shedding vs Work Queue — what decides between them?
points: Load Shedding — When you cannot slow the producer, drop work deliberately by priority.
Work Queue — A durable queue absorbs bursts; pair with backpressure so 'burst' cannot silently become 'forever'.

questions.prompt: Backpressure appears in 6 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Web Crawler — Politeness limits and frontier depth bound how fast the crawler pulls, so it neither melts a target site nor outruns its own parsers.
Design a Distributed Message Queue — Producers are slowed when partitions cannot absorb writes, because the alternative is unbounded broker storage followed by a hard failure.
Design an LLM Inference Platform — Queue depth signals the admission controller to reject or shed, rather than accumulating requests that will time out before a GPU frees up.
Design an Observability Platform — Ingest pushes back on agents when the pipeline saturates — dropping telemetry is preferable to the observability platform collapsing under it.
Design a Webhook Delivery System — A slow or dead receiver must not consume unbounded delivery capacity; per-endpoint concurrency limits stop one customer starving the rest.

Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — Per-tenant concurrency caps keep one bank's overnight backfill from consuming every worker slot, because the shared ceiling is model and vendor spend rather than CPU.
